Exponential Deterministic Query Complexity
of Goldstein Stationarity

Yixi Ding ††thanks: LSEC, ICMSEC, Academy of Mathematics and Systems Science, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100190, China; University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100049, China. Email: dingyixi@amss.ac.cn.    Ya-Xiang Yuan ††thanks: LSEC, ICMSEC, Academy of Mathematics and Systems Science, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100190, China. Email: yyx@lsec.cc.ac.cn.
Abstract

We study the deterministic query complexity of finding approximate Goldstein stationary points of globally Lipschitz functions that may be nonsmooth and nonconvex. Under prescribed bounds on the Lipschitz constant and on the difference between the initial function value and the infimum, we prove a lower bound on the worst-case number of oracle calls that is exponential in the dimension at fixed sufficiently small accuracy parameters. The result holds for a local oracle and gives explicit dependence on the accuracy parameters. A complementary deterministic algorithm using only function values gives an exponential upper bound, establishing the exponential order in the dimension in this regime. For a coarser stationarity requirement, we also give a deterministic first-order algorithm with a dimension-free query bound. Thus, the dimension dependence differs between the two accuracy regimes.

Key words. Goldstein stationarity, deterministic oracle complexity, nonsmooth nonconvex optimization, local oracles

MSC codes. 90C60, 90C56, 68Q25

1.  Introduction

Nonsmooth nonconvex optimization problems arise, for example, in piecewise affine models and neural networks with nonsmooth activation functions [8, 19]. For these problems, approximate stationarity provides a target that is weaker than global optimality. Unlike in smooth optimization, where a small gradient norm gives a natural measure of stationarity, the nonsmooth setting requires care in choosing a stationarity criterion for which finite-time guarantees are possible.

We consider a globally Lipschitz objective f:ℝd→ℝf:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R} that is bounded below, without imposing convexity or smoothness. For objectives with a Lipschitz continuous gradient, gradient descent admits finite bounds on the number of gradient evaluations needed to obtain a small gradient norm. These bounds are independent of dd when the gradient Lipschitz constant, initial function-value gap, and required accuracy are fixed [19, 8]. For a merely Lipschitz objective, however, asking for a small Clarke subgradient at the reported point can preclude a uniform finite-query guarantee over the function class [21, 15]. Thus, simply replacing the gradient by a generalized derivative does not resolve the computational difficulty. Goldstein’s stationarity condition relaxes this pointwise requirement by allowing a convex combination of subgradients at nearby points [7]. More precisely, a point 𝐱\mathbf{x} is (δ,ϵ)(\delta,\epsilon)-Goldstein stationary if a convex combination of Clarke subgradients at points within distance δ>0\delta>0 of 𝐱\mathbf{x} has norm at most ϵ>0\epsilon>0. Thus, δ\delta determines the neighborhood from which subgradients are taken, whereas ϵ\epsilon sets the allowable norm of such a convex combination. Section 2 gives the formal definitions.

This condition has a direct connection to descent. Goldstein’s method uses a minimum-norm element of the convex hull of nearby subgradients: either its norm is small, or its negative direction yields a decrease in the objective [7]. The difficulty is to obtain enough information to choose such a direction from finitely many oracle calls. A first-order oracle at one point does not supply the convex hull of subgradients throughout a neighborhood. Consequently, a bound on the number of these conceptual descent steps does not by itself give a bound on oracle queries. Randomized first-order algorithms address this difficulty. For any fixed failure probability γ∈(0,1)\gamma\in(0,1), they can find a (δ,ϵ)(\delta,\epsilon)-Goldstein stationary point with probability at least 1−γ1-\gamma using O~​(δ−1​ϵ−3)\widetilde{O}(\delta^{-1}\epsilon^{-3}) oracle calls, under fixed Lipschitz and initial-gap bounds; see Davis et al. [5, Theorem 6] and Tian, Zhou, and So [20, Theorem 3.4]. Here O~\widetilde{O} suppresses logarithmic factors. Thus, for any fixed success probability below one, the query complexity is polynomially bounded in dd, δ−1\delta^{-1}, and ϵ−1\epsilon^{-1}, and is in fact independent of dd. These guarantees use exact first-order information and do not require a Lipschitz continuous gradient.

For deterministic first-order algorithms, Kornowski and Shamir [14] and Jordan et al. [8] prove lower bounds on the worst-case number of oracle calls that grow linearly with dd at sufficiently small fixed accuracy parameters. Tian and So [19] obtain a dimension-dependent lower bound even with access to a more informative local oracle. These results establish a limitation of deterministic algorithms, rather than only of a particular way to remove random sampling from an existing method. They do not, however, determine whether polynomial dependence on dd is possible. Jordan et al. [8] asked whether a deterministic first-order algorithm can find a (δ,ϵ)(\delta,\epsilon)-Goldstein stationary point with a number of oracle calls polynomial jointly in dd, δ−1\delta^{-1}, and ϵ−1\epsilon^{-1}. At fixed accuracy parameters, the distinction between polynomial and exponential dimension dependence remains important even after a dimension-free guarantee has been ruled out. Our results address this question for the general Lipschitz function class.

1.1.  Contributions

Let L>0L>0 bound the Lipschitz constant, and let Δ>0\Delta>0 bound the initial function-value gap f⁡(𝐱0)−infff(\mathbf{x}_{0})-\inf f at a prescribed initial point 𝐱0\mathbf{x}_{0}. Our results describe how deterministic query complexity depends on the dimension and the accuracy parameters. For 0<δ<Δ/L0<\delta<\Delta/L and 0<ϵ<L/30<\epsilon<L/3, Theorem 2.2 gives an explicit query complexity lower bound that is exponential in dd when L,Δ,δ,ϵL,\Delta,\delta,\epsilon are fixed. It applies to every deterministic algorithm using the local oracle defined in Tian and So [19]. Query locations are unrestricted, and the output need not have been queried. In particular, the result rules out a guarantee polynomial jointly in dd, δ−1\delta^{-1}, and ϵ−1\epsilon^{-1}. The proof uses a resisting-oracle construction that accommodates exponentially many query points; Sections 3–4 develop the construction and the argument.

A complementary deterministic algorithm uses only function values and gives an upper bound on the number of calls sufficient to find a (δ,ϵ)(\delta,\epsilon)-Goldstein stationary point for every admissible objective (Theorem 2.3). Together, the bounds give exp⁡(Θ⁡(d))\exp(\Theta(d)) query complexity for each fixed choice of L,Δ,δ,ϵL,\Delta,\delta,\epsilon in the range above; see Corollary 2.4 and the discussion following it. This determines the exponential order in dd, not the exact exponential base or the optimal joint dependence on dimension and accuracy.

The conclusion changes when the stationarity condition permits a larger value of ϵ\epsilon. For any δ>0\delta>0 and L/2<ϵ<LL/\sqrt{2}<\epsilon<L, Proposition 5.3 gives a deterministic first-order algorithm with a query bound independent of dd, without imposing smoothness. Here the first-order oracle returns a function value and one Clarke subgradient at each query. We refer to this range of ϵ\epsilon as coarse accuracy. Our bounds do not determine the dimension dependence for the intermediate range 1/3≤ϵ/L≤1/21/3\leq\epsilon/L\leq 1/\sqrt{2}.

1.2.  Related work

Randomized algorithms and stochastic oracles.

Burke, Lewis, and Overton [2] used convex combinations of sampled gradients and proved convergence under their regularity assumptions; Kiwiel [10] strengthened the analysis and studied a modified algorithm. Zhang et al. [21] obtained a dimension-free finite-time bound under Hadamard directional differentiability and a direction-dependent first-order oracle. Davis et al. [5] and Tian, Zhou, and So [20] developed randomized procedures for general Lipschitz functions using exact values and gradients at differentiability points. For zeroth-order information, Lin, Zheng, and Jordan [17] related uniform smoothing to the Goldstein subdifferential and developed randomized methods based on function values.

Random choices made by an algorithm are distinct from randomness in a stochastic oracle, which supplies sampled or noisy objective information. Cutkosky, Mehta, and Orabona [4] improved first-order query bounds through an online-to-non-convex conversion using unbiased stochastic gradients with bounded variance. Their neighborhood-stationarity condition requires the nearby points to average to the reported point and implies Goldstein stationarity for Lipschitz objectives. Kornowski and Shamir [16] obtained a zeroth-order query bound linear in dd for stochastic objectives accessed through sampled function values. The zeroth-order upper bound established below instead uses a deterministic algorithm and exact function values.

Deterministic algorithms and local information.

Tian and So [19] also prove a separate impossibility result for general zero-respecting algorithms, which do not explore coordinates along which the objective is locally constant near all preceding query points. Jordan et al. [8] show that removing function values precludes a uniform finite deterministic guarantee. Deterministic algorithms for smooth functions with logarithmic dependence on the gradient Lipschitz constant are given in [14, 8]. The present lower bound assumes no such smoothness parameter and places no restriction on query locations.

Concurrent work.

After we finished our work, we noticed there is a recent paper by Kornowski [12], which also establishes a lower bound on deterministic query complexity that is exponential in the dimension for Goldstein stationarity under a local oracle.

Other local targets and verification.

Kornowski and Shamir [15] prove a query complexity lower bound, exponential in the dimension, for approaching a point with a small Clarke subgradient, even with randomization and local information. That target is stronger than Goldstein stationarity: a convex combination of nearby subgradients can have small norm even when none of its constituent subgradients does. Kornowski, Padmanabhan, and Shamir [13] establish exponential difficulties for local guarantees formulated in terms of function values. Kalavasis, Stavropoulos, and Zampetakis [9] study verification complexity and derive search consequences, including an exponential lower bound on the number of zeroth-order queries for uniform Goldstein stationarity. Their result for ordinary Goldstein stationarity concerns the resolution of lattice-restricted queries. These results concern different combinations of stationarity target, oracle information, and query restrictions.

DC functions and quantitative assumptions.

Kong and Lewis [11] give a deterministic method for a class that includes differences of convex (DC) functions. Their guarantee depends on a directional oracle and an objective-specific measure of nonconvexity. The functions constructed in our lower-bound proof are also DC, so the comparison requires attention to the quantitative assumptions and the oracle information, not only to DC membership. Section 6 and Appendix C give this comparison.

Organization.

Section 2 defines the problem and oracle model and states the complexity bounds. Section 3 gives an overview of the construction and proves its geometric and interpolation properties. Section 4 then chooses the scalar parameters and proves the query complexity lower bound. Section 5 proves the upper bounds, and Section 6 discusses their scope and remaining questions. The appendices cover initialization and stopping, finite direction-net construction, DC structure, and a non-weakly-convex example.

2.  Problem formulation and complexity bounds

We recall the stationarity criterion, specify the function class and oracle model, and state the query complexity bounds.

2.1.  Notation and nonsmooth preliminaries

All vector norms are Euclidean, and ⟨𝐱,𝐲⟩=𝐱⊤​𝐲\left\langle\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\right\rangle=\mathbf{x}^{\top}\mathbf{y}. For r>0r>0 and 𝐱∈ℝd\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, write

𝔹r​(𝐱)={𝐲∈ℝd:‖𝐲−𝐱‖≤r},𝔹r∘​(𝐱)={𝐲∈ℝd:‖𝐲−𝐱‖<r}.\mathbb{B}_{r}(\mathbf{x})=\{\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:\|\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{x}\|\leq r\},\qquad\mathbb{B}_{r}^{\circ}(\mathbf{x})=\{\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:\|\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{x}\|<r\}.

The symbols 𝕊d−1\mathbb{S}^{d-1}, 𝟎\mathbf{0}, 𝐞j\mathbf{e}_{j}, and 𝐈\mathbf{I} denote the unit sphere, the zero vector, the standard basis vectors, and the identity matrix, respectively. The orthogonal complement of 𝐮\mathbf{u} is denoted by 𝐮⟂\mathbf{u}^{\perp}. For a scalar aa, write a+=max⁡{a,0}a_{+}=\max\{a,0\}. The symbols conv\mathrm{conv}, int\operatorname{int}, and arg⁡min⁡f\arg\min f denote convex hull, interior, and the set of global minimizers of ff, respectively. For a finite set SS, its cardinality is |S||S|. The notation Lip⁡(f)\Lip(f) denotes the least global Lipschitz constant. All logarithms are natural, and ⌊a⌋\lfloor a\rfloor denotes the greatest integer not exceeding aa. The notation exp⁡(Θ⁡(d))\exp(\Theta(d)) means upper and lower exponential bounds with positive exponent constants independent of dd.

For a locally Lipschitz function f:ℝd→ℝf:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}, a point 𝐱∈ℝd\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, and a direction 𝐯∈ℝd\mathbf{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, its Clarke generalized directional derivative f∘​(𝐱,𝐯)f^{\circ}(\mathbf{x};\mathbf{v}) and Clarke subdifferential ∂f⁡(𝐱)\partial f(\mathbf{x}) are defined by

f∘​(𝐱,𝐯)\displaystyle f^{\circ}(\mathbf{x};\mathbf{v}) =lim sup𝐲→𝐱t↓0f⁡(𝐲+t​𝐯)−f⁡(𝐲)t,\displaystyle=\limsup_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{y}\to\mathbf{x}\\ t\downarrow 0\end{subarray}}\frac{f(\mathbf{y}+t\mathbf{v})-f(\mathbf{y})}{t}, (2.1)
∂f⁡(𝐱)\displaystyle\partial f(\mathbf{x}) ={𝐠∈ℝd:⟨𝐠,𝐯⟩≤f∘​(𝐱,𝐯)​ for every ​𝐯∈ℝd}.\displaystyle=\{\mathbf{g}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:\left\langle\mathbf{g},\mathbf{v}\right\rangle\leq f^{\circ}(\mathbf{x};\mathbf{v})\text{ for every }\mathbf{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\}.

An unsubscripted ∂\partial always means this Clarke subdifferential.

The following three consequences of (2.1) are used in the construction. If f=hf=h on an open neighborhood of 𝐱\mathbf{x}, then their difference quotients coincide locally, giving

f∘​(𝐱,𝐯)=h∘​(𝐱,𝐯)for every ​𝐯,∂f⁡(𝐱)=∂h⁡(𝐱).f^{\circ}(\mathbf{x};\mathbf{v})=h^{\circ}(\mathbf{x};\mathbf{v})\quad\text{for every }\mathbf{v},\qquad\partial f(\mathbf{x})=\partial h(\mathbf{x}). (2.2)

For c>0c>0, positive scaling commutes with the limsup and the subdifferential inequalities, giving

∂(c​f)​(𝐱)=c​∂f⁡(𝐱).\partial(cf)(\mathbf{x})=c\,\partial f(\mathbf{x}). (2.3)

For an affine function h⁡(𝐱)=⟨𝐚,𝐱⟩+bh(\mathbf{x})=\left\langle\mathbf{a},\mathbf{x}\right\rangle+b, where 𝐚∈ℝd\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and b∈ℝb\in\mathbb{R},

∂h⁡(𝐱)={𝐚}.\partial h(\mathbf{x})=\{\mathbf{a}\}. (2.4)

For δ>0\delta>0, define the Goldstein subdifferential by

∂δf⁡(𝐱)=conv⁡(⋃𝐲∈𝔹δ​(𝐱)∂f⁡(𝐲)).\partial_{\delta}f(\mathbf{x})=\mathrm{conv}\left(\bigcup_{\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{B}_{\delta}(\mathbf{x})}\partial f(\mathbf{y})\right). (2.5)

For ϵ>0\epsilon>0, a point 𝐱\mathbf{x} is (δ,ϵ)(\delta,\epsilon)-Goldstein stationary if

dist⁡(𝟎,∂δf⁡(𝐱)):=inf𝐠∈∂δf⁡(𝐱)‖𝐠‖≤ϵ.\mathrm{dist}(\mathbf{0},\partial_{\delta}f(\mathbf{x})):=\inf_{\mathbf{g}\in\partial_{\delta}f(\mathbf{x})}\|\mathbf{g}\|\leq\epsilon. (2.6)

Thus, δ\delta is a neighborhood radius, while ϵ\epsilon bounds the distance from the origin to ∂δf⁡(𝐱)\partial_{\delta}f(\mathbf{x}). We follow the parameter order of Jordan et al. [8]. The same condition is called (ϵ,δ)(\epsilon,\delta)-Goldstein approximate stationarity, or (ϵ,δ)(\epsilon,\delta)-GAS, by Tian and So [19, Definition 3]. The upper-bound argument will use a minimum-norm element of this set.

Lemma 2.1 (Compactness of the Goldstein subdifferential).

If ff is globally LL-Lipschitz, then ∂δf⁡(𝐱)\partial_{\delta}f(\mathbf{x}) is nonempty, compact, and convex, and is contained in 𝔹L​(𝟎)\mathbb{B}_{L}(\mathbf{0}), for every 𝐱∈ℝd\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and δ>0\delta>0.

Proof.

The Clarke subdifferential is nonempty and compact and lies in 𝔹L​(𝟎)\mathbb{B}_{L}(\mathbf{0}) [3, Proposition 2.1.2]. The graph over 𝔹δ​(𝐱)\mathbb{B}_{\delta}(\mathbf{x}) is a closed subset of the compact product 𝔹δ​(𝐱)×𝔹L​(𝟎)\mathbb{B}_{\delta}(\mathbf{x})\times\mathbb{B}_{L}(\mathbf{0}) and is therefore compact. Projecting onto the subgradient coordinate shows that ⋃𝐲∈𝔹δ​(𝐱)∂f⁡(𝐲)\bigcup_{\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{B}_{\delta}(\mathbf{x})}\partial f(\mathbf{y}) is nonempty and compact. In finite dimensions, its convex hull is compact and remains in 𝔹L​(𝟎)\mathbb{B}_{L}(\mathbf{0}). See also [6, Section 2] and [18, Proposition 2.3 and Corollary 2.13]. ∎

Consequently, the infimum in (2.6) is attained, and no additional closure is needed in (2.5).

2.2.  Function class, algorithms, and query counts

Fix a prescribed initial point 𝐱0∈ℝd\mathbf{x}_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. For L,Δ>0L,\Delta>0, let

ℱd(L,Δ;𝐱0)={f:ℝd→ℝ:|f⁡(𝐱)−f⁡(𝐲)|≤L​‖𝐱−𝐲‖for all ​𝐱,𝐲,inf𝐱∈ℝdf⁡(𝐱)>−∞,f⁡(𝐱0)−inf𝐱∈ℝdf⁡(𝐱)≤Δ}.\mathcal{F}_{d}(L,\Delta;\mathbf{x}_{0})=\left\{f:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}:\begin{array}[]{l}|f(\mathbf{x})-f(\mathbf{y})|\leq L\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y}\|\quad\text{for all }\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y},\\ \inf_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}f(\mathbf{x})>-\infty,\\ f(\mathbf{x}_{0})-\inf_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}f(\mathbf{x})\leq\Delta\end{array}\right\}. (2.7)

Thus LL is an upper bound, not necessarily the least Lipschitz constant. No convexity, smoothness, weak convexity, or representation-size assumption is imposed.

A query is one call to an oracle at a specified point. The algorithm receives

d,L,Δ,𝐱0,δ,ϵ.d,\quad L,\quad\Delta,\quad\mathbf{x}_{0},\quad\delta,\quad\epsilon.

Its first oracle call is at 𝐱0\mathbf{x}_{0}. Following the local-oracle definition in Tian and So [19, Section 2.3 and Remark 1], an admissible response to a query at 𝐪\mathbf{q} is any locally Lipschitz function h𝐪:ℝd→ℝh_{\mathbf{q}}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R} satisfying

𝒪f​(𝐪)=h𝐪,h𝐪​(𝐲)=f⁡(𝐲)for all ​𝐲∈𝔹ν𝐪​(𝐪),ν𝐪>0.\mathcal{O}_{f}(\mathbf{q})=h_{\mathbf{q}},\qquad h_{\mathbf{q}}(\mathbf{y})=f(\mathbf{y})\quad\text{for all }\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{B}_{\nu_{\mathbf{q}}}(\mathbf{q}),\qquad\nu_{\mathbf{q}}>0. (2.8)

The radius ν𝐪\nu_{\mathbf{q}} is not returned. Two oracle responses provide the same local information at 𝐪\mathbf{q} if they agree on an open neighborhood of 𝐪\mathbf{q}. Neither response specifies a ball of known radius on which agreement with the objective is guaranteed.

A deterministic algorithm in this model may use all local information supplied by the oracle. Its internal computation, next query, stopping decision, and output depend only on the input and the local information in the previous oracle responses. In particular, replacing any finite collection of responses by functions that agree with them near the corresponding query points cannot change the subsequent computation before a new response is received. The neighborhoods need not have the same radius: the minimum of finitely many positive radii gives the common-radius condition in [19]. Information encoded solely outside these neighborhoods is not available to the algorithm.

Query locations are unrestricted in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, repeated queries are allowed, and the output need not be a queried point. The pair (f⁡(𝐪),∂f⁡(𝐪))(f(\mathbf{q}),\partial f(\mathbf{q})) depends only on the local information at 𝐪\mathbf{q}. An algorithm using function values and the entire Clarke subdifferential is therefore a special case. The same applies to local derivative information whenever it is defined. For a fixed objective, replacing responses by locally agreeing functions induces the same execution. The first-order upper bound in Section 5.4 is stated for an oracle returning a function value and one Clarke subgradient per call; the zeroth-order upper bound uses only function values.

Every oracle call is counted, including the initial one. Arbitrary finite internal computation with exact real information is allowed between calls; in particular, real arithmetic and comparisons are exact. An execution that computes forever without returning fails the finite-return requirement; no procedure for detecting such behavior is assumed. These are query-complexity conventions, not bounds on bit complexity or total running time. Finite preprocessing is allowed without any bound on its cost.

For a deterministic algorithm AA, a valid output is a (δ,ϵ)(\delta,\epsilon)-Goldstein stationary point. If the execution returns such a point in finite time, let τA​(f,𝐱0,δ,ϵ)\tau_{A}(f;\mathbf{x}_{0},\delta,\epsilon) be its total number of calls. If it never returns or returns an invalid point, set

τA​(f,𝐱0,δ,ϵ)=+∞.\tau_{A}(f;\mathbf{x}_{0},\delta,\epsilon)=+\infty.

Dependence on the fixed input parameters d,L,Δd,L,\Delta is suppressed in this notation. The optimal worst-case query complexity in this local model is

𝒯det​(d,L,Δ,δ,ϵ,𝐱0)=infAsupf∈ℱd​(L,Δ,𝐱0)τA​(f,𝐱0,δ,ϵ).\mathcal{T}_{\rm det}(d,L,\Delta,\delta,\epsilon;\mathbf{x}_{0})=\inf_{A}\ \sup_{f\in\mathcal{F}_{d}(L,\Delta;\mathbf{x}_{0})}\tau_{A}(f;\mathbf{x}_{0},\delta,\epsilon). (2.9)

The infimum is over deterministic algorithms in the model above. A uniform TT-call guarantee means that the same algorithm satisfies τA​(f,𝐱0,δ,ϵ)≤T\tau_{A}(f;\mathbf{x}_{0},\delta,\epsilon)\leq T for every admissible ff. Eventual success after more than TT calls gives a finite value τA>T\tau_{A}>T, not +∞+\infty. Receiving the TTth response still permits a return within budget; requesting another call does not. Appendix A treats algorithm-chosen initial points and optional pre-query returns.

2.3.  Main theorems

The lower bound uses the local oracle defined above, whereas the upper bound needs only values. Their comparison at fixed accuracy determines the exponential order in dd.

Theorem 2.2 (Accuracy-dependent query complexity lower bound).

Let d≥3d\geq 3, L,Δ>0L,\Delta>0, 𝐱0∈ℝd\mathbf{x}_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, and

0<δ<ΔL,0<ϵ<L3.0<\delta<\frac{\Delta}{L},\qquad 0<\epsilon<\frac{L}{3}.

For every integer T≥1T\geq 1 satisfying

T+1≤(L−ϵ2​ϵ)(d−2)/2,T+1\leq\left(\frac{L-\epsilon}{2\epsilon}\right)^{(d-2)/2}, (2.10)

and every deterministic algorithm AA in the local-oracle model above, there exists a fixed f∈ℱd​(L,Δ,𝐱0)f\in\mathcal{F}_{d}(L,\Delta;\mathbf{x}_{0}) with τA​(f,𝐱0,δ,ϵ)>T\tau_{A}(f;\mathbf{x}_{0},\delta,\epsilon)>T. Every point actually queried among the first TT calls, and the output if AA returns within TT calls, satisfies

dist⁡(𝟎,∂δf⁡(𝐪))>ϵ.\mathrm{dist}(\mathbf{0},\partial_{\delta}f(\mathbf{q}))>\epsilon.

Moreover, f⁡(𝐱0)=0f(\mathbf{x}_{0})=0, inff=−Δ\inf f=-\Delta, and int⁡(arg⁡min⁡f)≠∅\mathrm{int}(\arg\min f)\neq\varnothing.

The order of quantifiers is ∀A​∃f\forall A\,\exists f, with the input and budget fixed. A function ff witnessing failure of the algorithm within the budget is called a hard instance. It is allowed to depend on the algorithm as well as the fixed inputs and budget. Sections 3–4 give the construction and proof.

Theorem 2.3 (Deterministic zeroth-order query bound).

Let d≥1d\geq 1, L,Δ,δ>0L,\Delta,\delta>0, 𝐱0∈ℝd\mathbf{x}_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, and 0<ϵ<L0<\epsilon<L. A deterministic algorithm using only function values returns a (δ,ϵ)(\delta,\epsilon)-Goldstein stationary point of every f∈ℱd​(L,Δ,𝐱0)f\in\mathcal{F}_{d}(L,\Delta;\mathbf{x}_{0}) within

1+(2​Δδ​ϵ+1)​(1+4​Lϵ)d1+\left(\frac{2\Delta}{\delta\epsilon}+1\right)\left(1+\frac{4L}{\epsilon}\right)^{d} (2.11)

total calls. If ϵ≥L\epsilon\geq L, the initial point is already valid and the prescribed initial call suffices.

Since h𝐪​(𝐪)=f​(𝐪)h_{\mathbf{q}}(\mathbf{q})=f(\mathbf{q}), this also bounds (2.9). Both bounds hold when each oracle call returns the function value together with either the entire Clarke subdifferential or one Clarke subgradient: the upper bound ignores subgradients, and the lower-bound construction has singleton subdifferentials at every query used in the construction.

Corollary 2.4 (Fixed-accuracy exponential dimension dependence).

For every d≥4d\geq 4 and 𝐱0∈ℝd\mathbf{x}_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{d},

⌊(72)(d−2)/2⌋≤𝒯det​(d,1,1,12,18,𝐱0)≤1+33d+1.\left\lfloor\left(\frac{7}{2}\right)^{(d-2)/2}\right\rfloor\leq\mathcal{T}_{\rm det}\left(d,1,1,\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{1}{8};\mathbf{x}_{0}\right)\leq 1+33^{d+1}.

Consequently, the fixed-accuracy complexity is exp⁡(Θ⁡(d))\exp(\Theta(d)). There is no uniform deterministic bound that is a joint polynomial in (d,δ−1,ϵ−1)(d,\delta^{-1},\epsilon^{-1}) for the full function class, even with L=Δ=1L=\Delta=1.

Proof.

Set

Ed=(72)(d−2)/2,Td=⌊Ed⌋−1.E_{d}=\left(\frac{7}{2}\right)^{(d-2)/2},\qquad T_{d}=\lfloor E_{d}\rfloor-1.

For d≥4d\geq 4, Td≥1T_{d}\geq 1 and Td+1≤EdT_{d}+1\leq E_{d}. Theorem 2.2, applied with L=Δ=1L=\Delta=1, δ=1/2\delta=1/2, and ϵ=1/8\epsilon=1/8, gives for every AA an admissible ff with τA​(f)>Td\tau_{A}(f)>T_{d}. Since finite query counts are integers, taking the supremum over ff and then the infimum over AA gives the lower bound ⌊Ed⌋\lfloor E_{d}\rfloor.

At the same parameters, (2.11) gives

1+(32+1)​33d=1+33d+1.1+(32+1)33^{d}=1+33^{d+1}.

The inequality ⌊Ed⌋≥Ed/2\lfloor E_{d}\rfloor\geq E_{d}/2 then gives

d−22​log​72−log⁡2≤log⁡𝒯det​(d,1,1,12,18,𝐱0)≤(d+1)​log​33+log⁡2.\frac{d-2}{2}\log\frac{7}{2}-\log 2\leq\log\mathcal{T}_{\rm det}\left(d,1,1,\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{1}{8};\mathbf{x}_{0}\right)\leq(d+1)\log 33+\log 2.

This proves the exponential order. A joint polynomial guarantee in (d,δ−1,ϵ−1)(d,\delta^{-1},\epsilon^{-1}) would reduce to a polynomial in dd at (δ,ϵ)=(1/2,1/8)(\delta,\epsilon)=(1/2,1/8) and contradict the lower bound for sufficiently large dd. ∎

For general parameters with 0<ϵ<L/30<\epsilon<L/3 and 0<δ<Δ/L0<\delta<\Delta/L, the same integer-budget argument gives

𝒯det​(d,L,Δ,δ,ϵ,𝐱0)≥⌊(L−ϵ2​ϵ)(d−2)/2⌋(d≥3).\mathcal{T}_{\rm det}(d,L,\Delta,\delta,\epsilon;\mathbf{x}_{0})\geq\left\lfloor\left(\frac{L-\epsilon}{2\epsilon}\right)^{(d-2)/2}\right\rfloor\qquad(d\geq 3).

When the floor is at least two, apply Theorem 2.2 with a budget one smaller; when it is one, the initial call gives the bound. Together with Theorem 2.3, this yields exp⁡(Θ⁡(d))\exp(\Theta(d)) for fixed admissible parameters.

3.  A finite-set construction

The construction below assigns the prescribed affine local data to a finite point set satisfying a cardinality condition. Its scalar parameters remain free until Section 4.

3.1.  Overview of the construction

The main difficulty is to make a finite query history consistent with one objective while excluding Goldstein stationarity at every relevant point. Affine agreement near the queries fixes the oracle responses, but it is not enough: the neighborhood 𝔹δ​(𝐪)\mathbb{B}_{\delta}(\mathbf{q}) used in the stationarity condition can extend well beyond the region of affine agreement at 𝐪\mathbf{q}. The construction therefore uses an interpolant whose subgradients share a positive projection in one direction, even where its local formulas change.

Let S={𝐪1,…,𝐪N}⊂ℝdS=\{\mathbf{q}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{q}_{N}\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} be a finite set of NN distinct points at which both local affine agreement and Goldstein nonstationarity are required. Choose a unit vector 𝐮\mathbf{u} with first coordinate α>0\alpha>0 and with

|⟨𝐮,𝐪i−𝐪j⟩|≤γ​‖𝐪i−𝐪j‖(i≠j),|\langle\mathbf{u},\mathbf{q}_{i}-\mathbf{q}_{j}\rangle|\leq\gamma\|\mathbf{q}_{i}-\mathbf{q}_{j}\|\qquad(i\neq j),

where 0<α<γ<10<\alpha<\gamma<1. A Gaussian estimate and a union bound allow NN to be exponential in dd. This bound on inner products with the pairwise differences replaces the exact orthogonality to query-dependent subspaces used in [8, 19].

Let 𝐏=𝐈−𝐮𝐮⊤\mathbf{P}=\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{u}\mathbf{u}^{\top} be the orthogonal projection onto 𝐮⟂\mathbf{u}^{\perp}. For N≥2N\geq 2, the interpolant is

F⁡(𝐱)=min1≤i≤N⁡{𝐞1⊤​(𝐱−𝐪i)+β​(‖𝐏⁡(𝐱−𝐪i)‖−r)+},F(\mathbf{x})=\min_{1\leq i\leq N}\left\{\mathbf{e}_{1}^{\top}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{q}_{i})+\beta\bigl(\|\mathbf{P}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{q}_{i})\|-r\bigr)_{+}\right\},

where β>1/1−γ2\beta>1/\sqrt{1-\gamma^{2}} is the penalty coefficient and r>0r>0 is chosen in (3.9). Each indexed function is a branch. The norm in its penalty is the distance to the line through 𝐪i\mathbf{q}_{i} parallel to 𝐮\mathbf{u}; only the excess beyond rr is penalized. The bound on pairwise differences ensures that the iith branch is strictly smaller than the others near 𝐪i\mathbf{q}_{i}, where its own penalty vanishes. Hence F⁡(𝐱)=𝐞1⊤​(𝐱−𝐪i)F(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{e}_{1}^{\top}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{q}_{i}) there. For a singleton, the affine function itself suffices.

Every penalty is unchanged by translation along 𝐮\mathbf{u}, which gives

F⁡(𝐱+t​𝐮)=F⁡(𝐱)+α​t.F(\mathbf{x}+t\mathbf{u})=F(\mathbf{x})+\alpha t.

The Clarke defining inequalities in the directions 𝐮\mathbf{u} and −𝐮-\mathbf{u} then give ⟨𝐠,𝐮⟩=α\langle\mathbf{g},\mathbf{u}\rangle=\alpha for every 𝐠∈∂F⁡(𝐱)\mathbf{g}\in\partial F(\mathbf{x}). This common projection survives branch switches and convex combinations of subgradients. The bound LFL_{F} from Lemma 3.2 need not be the least Lipschitz constant of FF. Scaling by L/LFL/L_{F} and truncating below −Δ-\Delta produce the required objective. The condition δ<Δ/L\delta<\Delta/L keeps the truncation inactive on an open set containing each ball 𝔹δ​(𝐪i)\mathbb{B}_{\delta}(\mathbf{q}_{i}). The remaining task is to choose scalar parameters satisfying L​α/LF>ϵL\alpha/L_{F}>\epsilon while the bound on pairwise differences still permits the desired number of points.

These scalar parameters are fixed before any queries are generated. Each query at 𝐪\mathbf{q} receives the affine function (L/LF)​𝐞1⊤​(𝐱−𝐪)(L/L_{F})\mathbf{e}_{1}^{\top}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{q}), and only the answered part of the history is retained. If the algorithm returns within the budget, its output is added to SS, whether or not it was queried. The finite-set construction then supplies one objective realizing every retained response. When run on this fixed objective, the algorithm reproduces the retained history and the action following it by determinism and locality. Section 4 gives this resisting-oracle argument, including the case of an unqueried output.

3.2.  Choice of direction

The direction 𝐮\mathbf{u} must satisfy two competing requirements: its first coordinate must remain positive, while projection onto 𝐮⟂\mathbf{u}^{\perp} must retain enough of each pairwise difference to separate the affine branches. For 0<α<γ<10<\alpha<\gamma<1, write

sα:=1−α2,cγ:=1−γ2.s_{\alpha}:=\sqrt{1-\alpha^{2}},\qquad c_{\gamma}:=\sqrt{1-\gamma^{2}}.

The estimate below ensures that orthogonal projection preserves at least the fraction cγc_{\gamma} of the distance between any two points.

Lemma 3.1 (A direction with bounded inner products).

Let d≥3d\geq 3, 0<α<γ<10<\alpha<\gamma<1, and S={𝐪1,…,𝐪N}⊂ℝdS=\{\mathbf{q}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{q}_{N}\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} be a nonempty finite set of distinct points. If

N⁡(N−1)​(1−γ21−α2)(d−2)/2<1,N(N-1)\left(\frac{1-\gamma^{2}}{1-\alpha^{2}}\right)^{(d-2)/2}<1, (3.1)

⟨𝐮,𝐞1⟩=α,|⟨𝐮,𝐪i−𝐪j⟩|≤γ∥𝐪i−𝐪j∥(i≠j).\left\langle\mathbf{u},\mathbf{e}_{1}\right\rangle=\alpha,\qquad|\left\langle\mathbf{u},\mathbf{q}_{i}-\mathbf{q}_{j}\right\rangle|\leq\gamma\|\mathbf{q}_{i}-\mathbf{q}_{j}\|\quad(i\neq j). (3.2)

For N=1N=1, condition (3.1) holds automatically and the second requirement is empty.

𝐮=α​𝐞1+sα​𝐯.\mathbf{u}=\alpha\mathbf{e}_{1}+s_{\alpha}\mathbf{v}. (3.3)

Then ‖𝐮‖=1\|\mathbf{u}\|=1 and ⟨𝐮,𝐞1⟩=α\left\langle\mathbf{u},\mathbf{e}_{1}\right\rangle=\alpha. For a fixed unit vector 𝐰\mathbf{w}, define the set of choices that violate the inner-product bound by

ℰ(𝐰):={𝐯∈𝐞1⟂:∥𝐯∥=1,|⟨α𝐞1+sα𝐯,𝐰⟩|>γ}.\mathcal{E}(\mathbf{w}):=\left\{\mathbf{v}\in\mathbf{e}_{1}^{\perp}:\|\mathbf{v}\|=1,\ \bigl|\left\langle\alpha\mathbf{e}_{1}+s_{\alpha}\mathbf{v},\mathbf{w}\right\rangle\bigr|>\gamma\right\}.

3.3.  Construction of an auxiliary Lipschitz function

To preserve a common slope along 𝐮\mathbf{u}, each affine model is penalized only in the transverse directions. The penalty must make a branch uniquely active near its center without increasing the Lipschitz bound with the number of centers.

Lemma 3.2 (A Lipschitz function with prescribed local behavior).

Let S={𝐪1,…,𝐪N}⊂ℝdS=\{\mathbf{q}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{q}_{N}\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} be a nonempty finite set of distinct points, and let 𝐮\mathbf{u} satisfy (3.2) for 0<α<γ<10<\alpha<\gamma<1. Choose β>1/cγ\beta>1/c_{\gamma}, and define the unscaled Lipschitz bound

LF:=α2+(sα+β)2,sα=1−α2,cγ=1−γ2.L_{F}:=\sqrt{\alpha^{2}+(s_{\alpha}+\beta)^{2}},\qquad s_{\alpha}=\sqrt{1-\alpha^{2}},\quad c_{\gamma}=\sqrt{1-\gamma^{2}}. (3.6)

    F⁡(𝐱)=𝐞1⊤​(𝐱−𝐪i)F(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{e}_{1}^{\top}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{q}_{i}) on an open neighborhood of every 𝐪i\mathbf{q}_{i}. Consequently, F⁡(𝐪i)=0F(\mathbf{q}_{i})=0 and ∂F⁡(𝐪i)={𝐞1}\partial F(\mathbf{q}_{i})=\{\mathbf{e}_{1}\}.

For N≥2N\geq 2, the neighborhood in (i) can be the open ball 𝔹r∘​(𝐪i)\mathbb{B}_{r}^{\circ}(\mathbf{q}_{i}) for the common radius in (3.9).

4.  The deterministic query complexity lower bound

Increasing the penalty coefficient strengthens branch separation but raises LFL_{F}, reducing the projection after scaling. The parameter choice below satisfies the separation condition, the required projection bound, and the probability bound for all pairwise differences simultaneously. The scalar parameters must be fixed before the queries, because L/LFL/L_{F} appears in every oracle response.

4.1.  Choice of scalar parameters

Let d≥3d\geq 3, L>0L>0, and 0<ϵ<L/30<\epsilon<L/3. Let the integer T≥1T\geq 1 satisfy (2.10). There are scalars 0<α<γ<10<\alpha<\gamma<1 and β>1/cγ\beta>1/c_{\gamma}, depending only on d,L,ϵ,Td,L,\epsilon,T, for which LFL_{F} in (3.6) satisfies

4.2.  A resisting-oracle argument

With the affine responses prescribed, the finite-set construction gives one objective agreeing with the resulting finite history. Locality and determinism then reproduce that history on the fixed objective.

Proof of Theorem 2.2.

Fix the inputs, the budget TT, and a deterministic algorithm AA. Choose α,γ,β,LF\alpha,\gamma,\beta,L_{F} by Lemma 4.1. First consider a run of AA with prescribed oracle responses, without yet choosing an objective. At each query point 𝐪\mathbf{q}, let the oracle return

𝒪⁡(𝐪)=ℓ𝐪,ℓ𝐪​(𝐱)=LLF​𝐞1⊤​(𝐱−𝐪).\mathcal{O}(\mathbf{q})=\ell_{\mathbf{q}},\qquad\ell_{\mathbf{q}}(\mathbf{x})=\frac{L}{L_{F}}\mathbf{e}_{1}^{\top}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{q}).

The first call is at 𝐱0\mathbf{x}_{0} and is counted. These responses determine the subsequent computation, although 𝐮\mathbf{u} and the objective have not yet been chosen. Only a finite answered history will be realized, not an infinite sequence of prescribed responses. Retain the sequence of queries and responses up to a return, a request for call T+1T+1, or internal computation that never produces another query or return. There are three cases.

(i) Return within TT calls. If AA returns 𝐱^\widehat{\mathbf{x}} after 1≤m≤T1\leq m\leq T responses at 𝐪(1),…,𝐪(m)\mathbf{q}^{(1)},\ldots,\mathbf{q}^{(m)}, set

S={𝐪(1),…,𝐪(m),𝐱^}.S=\{\mathbf{q}^{(1)},\ldots,\mathbf{q}^{(m)},\widehat{\mathbf{x}}\}. (4.2)

The output is fixed by the answered history, even if it was not queried, and |S|≤m+1≤T+1|S|\leq m+1\leq T+1.

(ii) Request for call T+1T+1. Retain the TT answered locations and set S={𝐪(1),…,𝐪(T)}S=\{\mathbf{q}^{(1)},\ldots,\mathbf{q}^{(T)}\}. No response at the next requested point, and no inclusion of that point in SS, is needed: reproducing the request already excludes a return within TT calls.

(iii) No further query or return. If, after 1≤m≤T1\leq m\leq T responses, no further query or return is ever produced, set S={𝐪(1),…,𝐪(m)}S=\{\mathbf{q}^{(1)},\ldots,\mathbf{q}^{(m)}\}.

These cases exhaust the possible behavior before call T+1T+1; the argument does not require detecting nontermination. In every case 𝐪(1)=𝐱0∈S\mathbf{q}^{(1)}=\mathbf{x}_{0}\in S and 1≤N:=|S|≤T+11\leq N:=|S|\leq T+1. Repeated locations are removed only in forming the set, not from the query count.

A fixed objective. By (4.1),

N⁡(N−1)​(1−γ21−α2)(d−2)/2<1.N(N-1)\left(\frac{1-\gamma^{2}}{1-\alpha^{2}}\right)^{(d-2)/2}<1.

Proposition 3.3 therefore supplies 𝐮\mathbf{u}, FF, and the fixed function f⁡(𝐱)=max⁡{L​F​(𝐱)/LF,−Δ}f(\mathbf{x})=\max\{LF(\mathbf{x})/L_{F},-\Delta\} satisfying

f∈ℱd​(L,Δ,𝐱0),f⁡(𝐱0)=0,inff=−Δ,int⁡(arg⁡min⁡f)≠∅.f\in\mathcal{F}_{d}(L,\Delta;\mathbf{x}_{0}),\qquad f(\mathbf{x}_{0})=0,\qquad\inf f=-\Delta,\qquad\mathrm{int}(\arg\min f)\neq\varnothing. (4.3)

For every 𝐪∈S\mathbf{q}\in S,

(f⁡(𝐪),∂f⁡(𝐪))=(0,{L​𝐞1/LF}),dist⁡(𝟎,∂δf⁡(𝐪))≥L​α/LF>ϵ.\bigl(f(\mathbf{q}),\partial f(\mathbf{q})\bigr)=\bigl(0,\{L\mathbf{e}_{1}/L_{F}\}\bigr),\qquad\mathrm{dist}(\mathbf{0},\partial_{\delta}f(\mathbf{q}))\geq L\alpha/L_{F}>\epsilon. (4.4)

The local oracle requires neighborhood agreement: there is a common ρ>0\rho>0 such that f=ℓ𝐪f=\ell_{\mathbf{q}} on 𝔹ρ∘​(𝐪)\mathbb{B}_{\rho}^{\circ}(\mathbf{q}) for every 𝐪∈S\mathbf{q}\in S. Thus each prescribed response agrees with ff on the closed ball 𝔹ρ/2​(𝐪)\mathbb{B}_{\rho/2}(\mathbf{q}), as required by (2.8); the radius is not disclosed. Thus all retained oracle responses are consistent with this one fixed function. Fix an oracle that returns ℓ𝐪\ell_{\mathbf{q}} for 𝐪∈S\mathbf{q}\in S and ff itself elsewhere. All its responses are admissible, and both the objective and the representatives are now fixed.

Consistency of the executions. Run AA with this oracle and the same inputs. The first query and response are the same as in the run with prescribed responses. Inductively, once the two executions have received the same responses to the same queries, locality and determinism give identical internal computation and the same next action. If that action is another query in the retained history, its location lies in SS and receives the same affine response. If it is a return or the request for call T+1T+1, that action is reproduced. If the internal computation never produces another action, it is identical in both executions. This proves agreement through the retained history and the behavior immediately following it.

In case (i), the returned point is invalid by (4.2) and (4.4); hence τA​(f,𝐱0,δ,ϵ)=+∞\tau_{A}(f;\mathbf{x}_{0},\delta,\epsilon)=+\infty. Including an unqueried output in SS imposes no additional call. In case (ii), any valid eventual return requires at least T+1T+1 calls; otherwise τA=+∞\tau_{A}=+\infty. In case (iii), there is no finite return. Thus τA>T\tau_{A}>T in every case. Every point actually queried among the first TT calls belongs to SS and therefore satisfies the strict nonstationarity bound in (4.4). The remaining properties are (4.3). ∎

Because all queried points in the retained history are nonstationary, the argument also excludes a guarantee that merely one of the first TT queried points is stationary, without requiring the algorithm to identify it.

Range of the parameter estimate.

The value 1/31/3 is a limit of this parameter estimate, not a threshold established for the optimization problem. Indeed, γ>α\gamma>\alpha and β>1/cγ\beta>1/c_{\gamma} imply β>1/sα\beta>1/s_{\alpha}, whence

α2LF2<sα2​(1−sα2)1+3​sα2≤19.\frac{\alpha^{2}}{L_{F}^{2}}<\frac{s_{\alpha}^{2}(1-s_{\alpha}^{2})}{1+3s_{\alpha}^{2}}\leq\frac{1}{9}.

The last inequality is equivalent to (3​sα2−1)2≥0(3s_{\alpha}^{2}-1)^{2}\geq 0. These estimates therefore cannot certify a projection of L/3L/3 or larger.

5.  Deterministic upper bounds

Goldstein nonstationarity implies descent over a segment of length δ\delta. Lipschitz continuity allows the descent direction to be approximated by a finite net, and the initial gap bounds the number of accepted moves. This gives a deterministic zeroth-order method. When L/2<ϵ<LL/\sqrt{2}<\epsilon<L, one returned subgradient suffices to choose the trial direction.

5.1.  A finite direction net

An η\eta-net of the unit sphere approximates every unit direction to distance at most η\eta. The packing estimate below bounds its size; Appendix B gives a finite construction in the exact-real query model.

Lemma 5.1 (A finite direction net).

For every d≥1d\geq 1 and η>0\eta>0, there is a nonempty finite set 𝒱⊂𝕊d−1\mathcal{V}\subset\mathbb{S}^{d-1} such that

for every ​𝐯∈𝕊d−1​ there is ​𝐰∈𝒱​ with ​‖𝐯−𝐰‖≤η,\text{for every }\mathbf{v}\in\mathbb{S}^{d-1}\text{ there is }\mathbf{w}\in\mathcal{V}\text{ with }\|\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{w}\|\leq\eta, (5.1)

and

|𝒱|≤(1+2/η)d.|\mathcal{V}|\leq(1+2/\eta)^{d}. (5.2)

The set and its ordering can be constructed deterministically using finite internal computation, independently of ff, in the exact-real model of Section 2.

Proof.

For η≥2\eta\geq 2, a fixed unit vector suffices. For 0<η<20<\eta<2, let 𝐰1,…,𝐰M\mathbf{w}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{w}_{M} be unit vectors with pairwise distances greater than η\eta. The balls 𝔹η/2∘​(𝐰j)\mathbb{B}_{\eta/2}^{\circ}(\mathbf{w}_{j}) are disjoint and contained in 𝔹1+η/2∘​(𝟎)\mathbb{B}_{1+\eta/2}^{\circ}(\mathbf{0}). Comparing their volumes gives

M​(η/2)d≤(1+η/2)d,M≤(1+2/η)d.M(\eta/2)^{d}\leq(1+\eta/2)^{d},\qquad M\leq(1+2/\eta)^{d}.

Starting with a fixed unit vector, append a point at distance greater than η\eta from all previously selected points whenever one exists. The packing bound forces this process to stop, yielding (5.1) with the size bound (5.2).

For a deterministic implementation, one must decide whether another point can be added. Appendix B gives a finite decision test and selects an admissible point from a fixed dense rational enumeration whenever the test succeeds. The insertion order gives the required ordering; no query to ff is used. ∎

5.2.  A descent step of length δ\delta

A separating direction controls every subgradient along the corresponding segment in 𝔹δ​(𝐱)\mathbb{B}_{\delta}(\mathbf{x}). This permits a step of length δ\delta, rather than one whose admissible length depends on unknown local behavior.

Lemma 5.2 (Descent from Goldstein nonstationarity).

Let f:ℝd→ℝf:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R} be globally LL-Lipschitz, let δ>0\delta>0, and assume

dist⁡(𝟎,∂δf⁡(𝐱))>ϵ>0.\mathrm{dist}(\mathbf{0},\partial_{\delta}f(\mathbf{x}))>\epsilon>0.

Then there is a unit vector 𝐯∈ℝd\mathbf{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} such that

f⁡(𝐱−δ​𝐯)<f⁡(𝐱)−δ​ϵ.f(\mathbf{x}-\delta\mathbf{v})<f(\mathbf{x})-\delta\epsilon. (5.3)
Proof.

Let C=∂δf⁡(𝐱)C=\partial_{\delta}f(\mathbf{x}), which is nonempty, compact, and convex by Lemma 2.1, and choose a minimum-norm element 𝐠∗∈C\mathbf{g}_{*}\in C. For 𝐠∈C\mathbf{g}\in C and 0<s≤10<s\leq 1, minimality gives

0≤‖𝐠∗+s⁡(𝐠−𝐠∗)‖2−‖𝐠∗‖2=2​s​⟨𝐠∗,𝐠−𝐠∗⟩+s2​‖𝐠−𝐠∗‖2.0\leq\|\mathbf{g}_{*}+s(\mathbf{g}-\mathbf{g}_{*})\|^{2}-\|\mathbf{g}_{*}\|^{2}=2s\left\langle\mathbf{g}_{*},\mathbf{g}-\mathbf{g}_{*}\right\rangle+s^{2}\|\mathbf{g}-\mathbf{g}_{*}\|^{2}.

Dividing by ss and letting s↓0s\downarrow 0 yields ⟨𝐠∗,𝐠−𝐠∗⟩≥0\left\langle\mathbf{g}_{*},\mathbf{g}-\mathbf{g}_{*}\right\rangle\geq 0. Since ‖𝐠∗‖>ϵ\|\mathbf{g}_{*}\|>\epsilon, the unit vector 𝐯=𝐠∗/‖𝐠∗‖\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{g}_{*}/\|\mathbf{g}_{*}\| satisfies

⟨𝐠,𝐯⟩≥‖𝐠∗‖>ϵ(𝐠∈C).\left\langle\mathbf{g},\mathbf{v}\right\rangle\geq\|\mathbf{g}_{*}\|>\epsilon\qquad(\mathbf{g}\in C).

Lebourg’s mean value theorem [3, Theorem 2.3.7] gives a point 𝐳=𝐱−θ​δ​𝐯\mathbf{z}=\mathbf{x}-\theta\delta\mathbf{v}, θ∈(0,1)\theta\in(0,1), and a vector 𝐠∈∂f⁡(𝐳)\mathbf{g}\in\partial f(\mathbf{z}) such that

f⁡(𝐱−δ​𝐯)−f⁡(𝐱)=−δ⁡⟨𝐠,𝐯⟩.f(\mathbf{x}-\delta\mathbf{v})-f(\mathbf{x})=-\delta\left\langle\mathbf{g},\mathbf{v}\right\rangle.

Since 𝐳∈𝔹δ​(𝐱)\mathbf{z}\in\mathbb{B}_{\delta}(\mathbf{x}), the vector satisfies 𝐠∈C\mathbf{g}\in C. The separation inequality therefore gives

f⁡(𝐱−δ​𝐯)−f⁡(𝐱)≤−δ​‖𝐠∗‖<−δ​ϵ.f(\mathbf{x}-\delta\mathbf{v})-f(\mathbf{x})\leq-\delta\|\mathbf{g}_{*}\|<-\delta\epsilon.

∎

5.3.  Direction-net descent and query complexity

Each iteration scans the same ordered net. Its radius is chosen to retain at least half of the decrease in Lemma 5.2. Values at accepted trial points are retained for the next iteration.

For 0<ϵ<L0<\epsilon<L, set η=ϵ/(2​L)\eta=\epsilon/(2L) and fix an ordered net 𝒱=(𝐰1,…,𝐰M)\mathcal{V}=(\mathbf{w}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{w}_{M}) from Lemma 5.1, with

M≤(1+2/η)d=(1+4​Lϵ)d.M\leq(1+2/\eta)^{d}=\left(1+\frac{4L}{\epsilon}\right)^{d}. (5.4)

Algorithm 1 queries every direction in the ordered net, then moves along the first one giving a decrease of at least δ​ϵ/2\delta\epsilon/2. If no direction gives this decrease, it returns the current point.

Proof of Theorem 2.3.

First, consider 0<ϵ<L0<\epsilon<L. Lemma 5.1 and Appendix B make the preprocessing finite and deterministic. The stored value is always a=f⁡(𝐱)a=f(\mathbf{x}), because accepted trial values are reused.

If 𝐱\mathbf{x} is not (δ,ϵ)(\delta,\epsilon)-Goldstein stationary, Lemma 5.2 gives a unit vector 𝐯\mathbf{v} satisfying (5.3). Choose 𝐰j\mathbf{w}_{j} with ‖𝐰j−𝐯‖≤η\|\mathbf{w}_{j}-\mathbf{v}\|\leq\eta. Then

f⁡(𝐱−δ​𝐰j)\displaystyle f(\mathbf{x}-\delta\mathbf{w}_{j}) ≤f⁡(𝐱−δ​𝐯)+L​δ​‖𝐰j−𝐯‖\displaystyle\leq f(\mathbf{x}-\delta\mathbf{v})+L\delta\|\mathbf{w}_{j}-\mathbf{v}\|
<f⁡(𝐱)−δ​ϵ+L​δ​η=f⁡(𝐱)−δ​ϵ/2.\displaystyle<f(\mathbf{x})-\delta\epsilon+L\delta\eta=f(\mathbf{x})-\delta\epsilon/2.

Thus j∈Jj\in J. The stopping condition J=∅J=\varnothing therefore certifies stationarity.

Each accepted move decreases the value by at least δ​ϵ/2\delta\epsilon/2. Let 𝐱(m)\mathbf{x}^{(m)} denote the point reached after mm accepted moves. For every finite mm,

m​δ​ϵ2≤f⁡(𝐱0)−f⁡(𝐱(m))≤f⁡(𝐱0)−inff≤Δ.m\frac{\delta\epsilon}{2}\leq f(\mathbf{x}_{0})-f(\mathbf{x}^{(m)})\leq f(\mathbf{x}_{0})-\inf f\leq\Delta.

Consequently,

m≤2​Δδ​ϵ.m\leq\frac{2\Delta}{\delta\epsilon}. (5.5)

Since every scan is finite, the move bound (5.5) forces termination. There are mm successful scans and one final unsuccessful scan. Counting the initial call and all MM trials in each scan, and using (5.4), gives

τA​(f,𝐱0,δ,ϵ)\displaystyle\tau_{A}(f;\mathbf{x}_{0},\delta,\epsilon) ≤1+(m+1)​M\displaystyle\leq 1+(m+1)M
≤1+(2​Δδ​ϵ+1)​(1+4​Lϵ)d.\displaystyle\leq 1+\left(\frac{2\Delta}{\delta\epsilon}+1\right)\left(1+\frac{4L}{\epsilon}\right)^{d}.

Repeated queries are charged again in this count; reusing stored values cannot increase it.

If ϵ≥L\epsilon\geq L, Lemma 2.1 gives dist⁡(𝟎,∂δf⁡(𝐱0))≤L≤ϵ\mathrm{dist}(\mathbf{0},\partial_{\delta}f(\mathbf{x}_{0}))\leq L\leq\epsilon. The prescribed initial call followed by a return therefore suffices. ∎

The separating direction is used only in the analysis. The algorithm compares values, and its stopping test is sufficient but not necessary for stationarity. An accepted move is not excluded at a stationary iterate and remains subject to the same decrease bound.

5.4.  A first-order bound for coarse accuracy

A single subgradient need not point in a useful descent direction. When L/2<ϵ<LL/\sqrt{2}<\epsilon<L, however, an unsuccessful trial certifies stationarity: the current subgradient and one subgradient on the trial segment have an average of sufficiently small norm. The oracle returns f⁡(𝐱)f(\mathbf{x}) and one 𝐠∈∂f⁡(𝐱)\mathbf{g}\in\partial f(\mathbf{x}). The guarantee holds for every valid subgradient selection. No effective extraction from an arbitrary local-function representation is assumed.

Proposition 5.3 (Dimension-free first-order query bound).

Let d≥1d\geq 1, L,Δ,δ>0L,\Delta,\delta>0, 𝐱0∈ℝd\mathbf{x}_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, and L/2<ϵ<LL/\sqrt{2}<\epsilon<L. Algorithm 2 returns a (δ,ϵ)(\delta,\epsilon)-Goldstein stationary point of every f∈ℱd​(L,Δ,𝐱0)f\in\mathcal{F}_{d}(L,\Delta;\mathbf{x}_{0}) within

2+Δ​Lδ⁡(2​ϵ2−L2)2+\frac{\Delta L}{\delta(2\epsilon^{2}-L^{2})} (5.6)

first-order oracle calls.

Set sdec=(2​ϵ2−L2)/L>0s_{\mathrm{dec}}=(2\epsilon^{2}-L^{2})/L>0. The algorithm tries a step of length δ\delta opposite to the returned subgradient and accepts it only when the decrease exceeds δ​sdec\delta s_{\mathrm{dec}}.

Proof.

The stored data satisfy a=f⁡(𝐱)a=f(\mathbf{x}) and 𝐠∈∂f⁡(𝐱)\mathbf{g}\in\partial f(\mathbf{x}). If ‖𝐠‖≤ϵ\|\mathbf{g}\|\leq\epsilon, then ∂f⁡(𝐱)⊆∂δf⁡(𝐱)\partial f(\mathbf{x})\subseteq\partial_{\delta}f(\mathbf{x}) certifies the return.

Otherwise, let 𝐯=𝐠/‖𝐠‖\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{g}/\|\mathbf{g}\| and 𝐲=𝐱−δ​𝐯\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{x}-\delta\mathbf{v}. If the trial gives f⁡(𝐱)−f⁡(𝐲)≤δ​sdecf(\mathbf{x})-f(\mathbf{y})\leq\delta s_{\mathrm{dec}}, Lebourg’s mean value theorem gives 𝐳\mathbf{z} in the open segment from 𝐱\mathbf{x} to 𝐲\mathbf{y} and 𝐡∈∂f⁡(𝐳)\mathbf{h}\in\partial f(\mathbf{z}) such that

f⁡(𝐲)−f⁡(𝐱)=−δ⁡⟨𝐡,𝐯⟩,⟨𝐡,𝐯⟩≤sdec.f(\mathbf{y})-f(\mathbf{x})=-\delta\left\langle\mathbf{h},\mathbf{v}\right\rangle,\qquad\left\langle\mathbf{h},\mathbf{v}\right\rangle\leq s_{\mathrm{dec}}.

Both 𝐠\mathbf{g} and 𝐡\mathbf{h} belong to ∂δf⁡(𝐱)\partial_{\delta}f(\mathbf{x}) and have norm at most LL. Their average belongs to the same convex set, and

‖𝐠+𝐡2‖2\displaystyle\left\|\frac{\mathbf{g}+\mathbf{h}}{2}\right\|^{2} =‖𝐠‖2+‖𝐡‖2+2​⟨𝐠,𝐡⟩4\displaystyle=\frac{\|\mathbf{g}\|^{2}+\|\mathbf{h}\|^{2}+2\left\langle\mathbf{g},\mathbf{h}\right\rangle}{4}
≤2​L2+2​‖𝐠‖​sdec4\displaystyle\leq\frac{2L^{2}+2\|\mathbf{g}\|s_{\mathrm{dec}}}{4}
≤2​L2+2​L​sdec4=ϵ2.\displaystyle\leq\frac{2L^{2}+2Ls_{\mathrm{dec}}}{4}=\epsilon^{2}.

Here sdec>0s_{\mathrm{dec}}>0 justifies replacing ‖𝐠‖\|\mathbf{g}\| by LL. The return is therefore valid. The vector 𝐡\mathbf{h} is supplied by Lebourg’s theorem, not by the query at the endpoint. It need not equal 𝐠𝐲\mathbf{g}_{\mathbf{y}}, and the algorithm does not compute it.

Every accepted move decreases the value by more than δ​sdec\delta s_{\mathrm{dec}}. Thus any finite number mm of accepted moves satisfies

m​δ​sdec≤f⁡(𝐱0)−inff≤Δ,m≤Δδ​sdec.m\delta s_{\mathrm{dec}}\leq f(\mathbf{x}_{0})-\inf f\leq\Delta,\qquad m\leq\frac{\Delta}{\delta s_{\mathrm{dec}}}.

Finite work in each iteration and this bound force termination. There is one initial call, one call per accepted move, and at most one final unsuccessful trial, giving at most m+2m+2 calls and hence (5.6). ∎

As ϵ↓L/2\epsilon\downarrow L/\sqrt{2}, the denominator in (5.6) vanishes. The argument gives no guarantee at the endpoint and does not establish optimal behavior near it.

6.  Conclusions and discussion

For fixed positive L,Δ,δL,\Delta,\delta with δ<Δ/L\delta<\Delta/L and a fixed ratio ϵ/L∈(0,1/3)\epsilon/L\in(0,1/3), deterministic query complexity is exponential in dimension, even in the local-oracle model of Section 2. Function values alone suffice for the same exponential order. In contrast, the first-order method has a dimension-free query bound when L/2<ϵ<LL/\sqrt{2}<\epsilon<L.

6.1.  Accuracy and information

The dependence on accuracy remains unresolved in part. The present bounds do not determine the dimension dependence for 1/3≤ϵ/L≤1/21/3\leq\epsilon/L\leq 1/\sqrt{2}, nor do they match the joint dependence on dimension and accuracy. Even at the parameters of Corollary 2.4, the exponential constants are 12​log⁡(7/2)\tfrac{1}{2}\log(7/2) and log⁡33\log 33. The calculation after Theorem 2.2 limits the projection estimate for the present construction to ϵ<L/3\epsilon<L/3; it does not establish a transition in the optimization problem. One question is whether the common projection captures the full distance of the Goldstein subdifferential from the origin.

The lower bound is insensitive to the choice between full local information and a value with one Clarke subgradient, because the constructed objective is affine near every queried point in the construction and has a singleton subdifferential there. The zeroth-order upper bound works in both models.

Determinism is essential to the resisting-oracle argument: the prescribed responses fix the history. The construction applied to different random seeds is not required to produce the same objective. Lemma 3.1 therefore does not provide a fixed hard instance with a failure probability for a randomized algorithm.

The bounds concern exact queries, not total computation. No upper bound on direction-net preprocessing time is claimed, and the number of branches in the hard instance depends on the budget. Its interpolation radius can be arbitrarily small when queries are close, although LFL_{F} and the common projection do not depend on that radius. No representation-size bound, minimum feature size, or gradient Lipschitz bound is assumed.

6.2.  Quantitative regularity

Local affine agreement does not make the hard family globally smooth. Appendix D gives a two-branch member that is not weakly convex for any finite parameter. Results requiring smoothness or weak convexity therefore do not cover the whole family.

Every finite hard instance is nevertheless DC by Appendix C. In comparing with Kong and Lewis [11], the relevant issue is quantitative nonconvexity, not DC membership alone. Their directional oracle returns values, directional derivatives, and direction-dependent vectors. The complexity depends on an objective-specific nonconvexity modulus Λ⁡(δ)\Lambda(\delta) defined through one-dimensional restrictions. To relate it to a DC decomposition, define

MDC​(f)=inf{Lip⁡(q):q​ is convex and ​f+q​ is convex}.M_{\rm DC}(f)=\inf\{\Lip(q):q\text{ is convex and }f+q\text{ is convex}\}.

Here a feasible qq is a convex correction, Lip⁡(q)=+∞\Lip(q)=+\infty if it is not globally Lipschitz, and inf∅=+∞\inf\varnothing=+\infty. Proposition 6.3 of Kong and Lewis [11] gives Λ⁡(δ)≤Lip⁡(q)\Lambda(\delta)\leq\Lip(q) for every Lipschitz convex correction, and hence Λ⁡(δ)≤MDC​(f)\Lambda(\delta)\leq M_{\rm DC}(f). Appendix C gives

MDC​(f)≤L⁡(N−1).M_{\rm DC}(f)\leq L(N-1).

This estimate comes from one decomposition. It neither proves that an intrinsic nonconvexity parameter grows with NN nor bounds that parameter in terms of LL alone. Estimating MDC​(f)M_{\rm DC}(f) over all corrections would separate the cost of this representation from the objective’s intrinsic nonconvexity. More broadly, it remains to identify quantitative structural assumptions under which a specified oracle admits polynomial dimension dependence.

Appendix A Initial-point conventions and stopping

The following observations relate the prescribed-initial-point model to other initialization and stopping conventions. Choosing the initial point before receiving oracle information incurs no query loss; a free initial response shifts the count by one.

Proposition A.1 (Transfer to an algorithm-chosen initial point).

Consider a deterministic algorithm that chooses its initial point from (d,L,Δ,δ,ϵ)(d,L,\Delta,\delta,\epsilon) before seeing any oracle information, makes its first query there, and counts that call. A uniform TT-call guarantee under that convention induces a uniform TT-call guarantee in the fixed-initial-point model at the particular initial point it chooses. Consequently, Theorem 2.2, which holds for every prescribed 𝐱0\mathbf{x}_{0}, transfers to that convention without losing a query.

Proof.

Fix the input parameters and the algorithm. If preprocessing does not terminate, there is no finite-return guarantee. Otherwise the chosen initial point 𝐱0A\mathbf{x}_{0}^{A} and the internal state before the first query are determined by the input alone. In the prescribed-initial-point model with 𝐱0=𝐱0A\mathbf{x}_{0}=\mathbf{x}_{0}^{A}, perform the same preprocessing and follow the algorithm. The two executions coincide on every f∈ℱd​(L,Δ,𝐱0A)f\in\mathcal{F}_{d}(L,\Delta;\mathbf{x}_{0}^{A}), with the same charged first call. A uniform TT-call guarantee would therefore contradict Theorem 2.2 at this prescribed point. ∎

Thus the algorithm-chosen convention in [8, Section 2] incurs no query loss in applying the lower bound.

Free initial responses.

If the initial response at 𝐱0\mathbf{x}_{0} is free and only JJ subsequent calls are counted, charge once for that response to obtain the convention used here. Conversely, giving the initial response for free removes precisely that call. Hence,

T=J+1,T+1=J+2.T=J+1,\qquad T+1=J+2.

The set SS used in the construction has at most J+2J+2 points: the initial point, JJ subsequent locations, and a possible unqueried output. At the fixed accuracy parameters of Corollary 2.4, the lower bound on additional calls is therefore ⌊(7/2)(d−2)/2⌋−1\lfloor(7/2)^{(d-2)/2}\rfloor-1, leaving the exponential order unchanged.

Before the initial call.

Allowing a return before the initial call does not change the lower bound. Such an output 𝐱^\widehat{\mathbf{x}} is fixed by the input alone. For a budget covered by Theorem 2.2, choose the parameters of Lemma 4.1 and take

S={𝐱0,𝐱^}.S=\{\mathbf{x}_{0},\widehat{\mathbf{x}}\}.

This set has at most two distinct points, and hence at most T+1T+1. Proposition 3.3 applies and gives an admissible objective with

dist⁡(𝟎,∂δf⁡(𝐱^))≥L​αLF>ϵ.\mathrm{dist}(\mathbf{0},\partial_{\delta}f(\widehat{\mathbf{x}}))\geq\frac{L\alpha}{L_{F}}>\epsilon.

The no-query execution returns that same invalid point.

If pre-query computation never terminates, it fails on every admissible objective, including the zero function. Otherwise the initial call is reached and the proof of Theorem 2.2 applies. Only the stopping convention changes.

Appendix B Finite deterministic construction of the direction net

The packing argument bounds the number of net points but does not determine when the sphere is covered. A finite decision test and a deterministic selection rule complete the construction. Both are independent of ff; computational efficiency is not required.

For d=1d=1, use the ordered set (−𝐞1,𝐞1)(-\mathbf{e}_{1},\mathbf{e}_{1}) when 0<η<20<\eta<2, and the singleton {𝐞1}\{\mathbf{e}_{1}\} when η≥2\eta\geq 2. Their cardinalities satisfy the bound in Lemma 5.1. Assume d≥2d\geq 2 below.

B.1.  Rational points on the sphere

For a rational vector 𝐭∈ℚd−1\mathbf{t}\in\mathbb{Q}^{d-1}, define

R⁡(𝐭)=(2​𝐭1+‖𝐭‖2,1−‖𝐭‖21+‖𝐭‖2)∈ℝd.R(\mathbf{t})=\left(\frac{2\mathbf{t}}{1+\|\mathbf{t}\|^{2}},\frac{1-\|\mathbf{t}\|^{2}}{1+\|\mathbf{t}\|^{2}}\right)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.

With s=‖𝐭‖2s=\|\mathbf{t}\|^{2}, direct substitution gives

‖R⁡(𝐭)‖2=4​s+(1−s)2(1+s)2=1.\|R(\mathbf{t})\|^{2}=\frac{4s+(1-s)^{2}}{(1+s)^{2}}=1.

Thus RR sends rational vectors to rational sphere points. The map extends continuously to ℝd−1\mathbb{R}^{d-1} and parametrizes the sphere except for −𝐞d-\mathbf{e}_{d}, with inverse 𝐭=𝐰′/(1+wd)\mathbf{t}=\mathbf{w}^{\prime}/(1+w_{d}) for 𝐰=(𝐰′,wd)\mathbf{w}=(\mathbf{w}^{\prime},w_{d}) and wd≠−1w_{d}\neq-1. Density of rational parameters shows that R⁡(ℚd−1)∪{−𝐞d}R(\mathbb{Q}^{d-1})\cup\{-\mathbf{e}_{d}\} is dense in the sphere. Enumerate ℚd−1\mathbb{Q}^{d-1} by increasing bounds on absolute numerators and positive denominators, using lexicographic order within each finite bound and skipping repetitions. Applying RR and inserting −𝐞d-\mathbf{e}_{d} at a fixed position gives a dense enumeration independent of the objective.

B.2.  A stopping test and finite termination

For an ordered set 𝒱=(𝐰1,…,𝐰M)\mathcal{V}=(\mathbf{w}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{w}_{M}) of selected rational points, test

∃𝐱∈ℝd:∑ℓ=1dxℓ2=1,∑ℓ=1d(xℓ−wj,ℓ)2>η2(j=1,…,M).\exists\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:\quad\sum_{\ell=1}^{d}x_{\ell}^{2}=1,\quad\sum_{\ell=1}^{d}(x_{\ell}-w_{j,\ell})^{2}>\eta^{2}\quad(j=1,\ldots,M). (B.1)

Here xℓx_{\ell} and wj,ℓw_{j,\ell} denote vector coordinates. For M=0M=0, only the sphere equation remains, and the test is true. With η\eta as a free real parameter, (B.1) is an existential formula with rational polynomial coefficients. Real quantifier elimination [1] gives an equivalent finite combination of polynomial sign conditions on η\eta. These can be evaluated by the exact arithmetic and comparisons allowed in Section 2, without querying ff.

If the test is false, 𝒱\mathcal{V} is an η\eta-net. If it is true, the set

U𝒱={𝐱∈𝕊d−1:∥𝐱−𝐰j∥>η for j=1,…,M}U_{\mathcal{V}}=\{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{S}^{d-1}:\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{w}_{j}\|>\eta\text{ for }j=1,\ldots,M\}

is nonempty and relatively open. It therefore contains a point of the dense enumeration. Append the first enumerated point satisfying the strict inequalities, and repeat the decision test. The search terminates because some admissible point has a finite index. Each selected set is strictly η\eta-separated and hence has size at most (1+2/η)d(1+2/\eta)^{d}. Since every decision and selection is finite, the procedure terminates with the required ordered net.

Appendix C Difference-of-convex structure of the hard family

A function is difference-of-convex (DC) if f=p−qf=p-q with pp and qq convex. Equivalently, qq is a convex correction making f+qf+q convex; it need not be unique. Each branch of the interpolant is convex, although their minimum need not be. Their sum gives a direct DC decomposition that also accommodates the lower truncation.

Proposition C.1 (The finite hard instance is DC).

Every finite hard instance produced by Proposition 3.3 is DC.

If N=1N=1, then the construction is

F⁡(𝐱)=𝐞1⊤​(𝐱−𝐪1),f⁡(𝐱)=max⁡{LLF​𝐞1⊤​(𝐱−𝐪1),−Δ},F(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{e}_{1}^{\top}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{q}_{1}),\qquad f(\mathbf{x})=\max\left\{\frac{L}{L_{F}}\mathbf{e}_{1}^{\top}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{q}_{1}),-\Delta\right\},

and ff is convex. Taking p=fp=f and q=0q=0 gives

Lip⁡(q)=0=L⁡(N−1),Lip⁡(p)≤L=L​N.\Lip(q)=0=L(N-1),\qquad\Lip(p)\leq L=LN.

If N≥2N\geq 2, let F1,…,FNF_{1},\ldots,F_{N} be the branches in (3.11), let F=mini⁡FiF=\min_{i}F_{i}, and define

H⁡(𝐱)=∑i=1NFi​(𝐱),K⁡(𝐱)=max⁡∑j≠i1≤i≤N⁡Fj​(𝐱).H(\mathbf{x})=\sum_{i=1}^{N}F_{i}(\mathbf{x}),\qquad K(\mathbf{x})=\max_{1\leq i\leq N}\sum_{j\neq i}F_{j}(\mathbf{x}).

Then HH and KK are convex and F=H−KF=H-K. Moreover, with

p⁡(𝐱)=max⁡{LLF​H​(𝐱),LLF​K​(𝐱)−Δ},q⁡(𝐱)=LLF​K​(𝐱),p(\mathbf{x})=\max\left\{\frac{L}{L_{F}}H(\mathbf{x}),\frac{L}{L_{F}}K(\mathbf{x})-\Delta\right\},\qquad q(\mathbf{x})=\frac{L}{L_{F}}K(\mathbf{x}),

the functions p,qp,q are convex and satisfy f=p−qf=p-q. The displayed decomposition satisfies

Lip⁡(q)≤L⁡(N−1),Lip⁡(p)≤L​N.\Lip(q)\leq L(N-1),\qquad\Lip(p)\leq LN.
Proof.

The case N=1N=1 is given in the statement. For N≥2N\geq 2, every branch is convex: its penalty is the maximum of a convex norm-minus-constant function and zero, and its remaining term is affine. Thus HH and KK are convex, and

K=maxi⁡(H−Fi)=H−mini⁡Fi=H−F.K=\max_{i}(H-F_{i})=H-\min_{i}F_{i}=H-F.

Substitution into (3.17) gives

f=max⁡{LLF​(H−K),−Δ}=max⁡{LLF​H,LLF​K−Δ}−LLF​K=p−q.f=\max\left\{\frac{L}{L_{F}}(H-K),-\Delta\right\}=\max\left\{\frac{L}{L_{F}}H,\frac{L}{L_{F}}K-\Delta\right\}-\frac{L}{L_{F}}K=p-q.

The functions pp and qq are convex. Since each FiF_{i} is LFL_{F}-Lipschitz, HH is N​LFNL_{F}-Lipschitz and KK is (N−1)​LF(N-1)L_{F}-Lipschitz. Scaling and taking the finite maximum give the claimed bounds on Lip⁡(p)\Lip(p) and Lip⁡(q)\Lip(q). ∎

Remark C.2 (Comparison with the Kong–Lewis modulus).

Using the notation and DC comparison in Section 6, the correction in Proposition C.1 gives

Λ⁡(δ)≤MDC​(f)≤Lip⁡(q)≤L⁡(N−1).\Lambda(\delta)\leq M_{\rm DC}(f)\leq\Lip(q)\leq L(N-1).

This is an upper bound only; it does not establish a lower bound proportional to NN for either intrinsic quantity.

For N≥2N\geq 2, the translation identity gives K⁡(𝐱+t​𝐮)=K⁡(𝐱)+(N−1)​α​tK(\mathbf{x}+t\mathbf{u})=K(\mathbf{x})+(N-1)\alpha t for the maximum of the branch sums defining KK. The displayed correction q=(L/LF)​Kq=(L/L_{F})K therefore satisfies

For the parameter choice in Lemma 4.1, α/LF>ϵ/L\alpha/L_{F}>\epsilon/L. Thus, for N≥2N\geq 2 and a fixed ratio ϵ/L>0\epsilon/L>0, the Lipschitz constant of this correction is bounded above and below by positive constants times L​NLN. These constants can depend on ϵ/L\epsilon/L, but not on dd or NN. The lower bound concerns only the displayed correction and does not compare it with all other admissible corrections. Estimating MDC​(f)M_{\rm DC}(f) over all corrections, or estimating Λ⁡(δ)\Lambda(\delta), requires a separate argument.

A two-branch member of the construction has a downward cusp along a line. Adding a quadratic leaves the jump in the one-sided derivatives unchanged and cannot make the restriction convex.

The projected distances are |t−a||t-a| and |t+a||t+a|. For |t|<a−r|t|<a-r,

F⁡(t​𝐞3)=2​min⁡{|t−a|−r,|t+a|−r}=2​(a−r)−2​|t|>0.F(t\mathbf{e}_{3})=2\min\{|t-a|-r,|t+a|-r\}=2(a-r)-2|t|>0.

Set L=Δ=1L=\Delta=1 and f⁡(𝐱)=max⁡{F⁡(𝐱)/LF,−1}f(\mathbf{x})=\max\{F(\mathbf{x})/L_{F},-1\}. The truncation is inactive on this interval, giving

f⁡(t​𝐞3)=2​(a−r)LF−2LF​|t|.f(t\mathbf{e}_{3})=\frac{2(a-r)}{L_{F}}-\frac{2}{L_{F}}|t|. (D.1)

For any finite ϱ≥0\varrho\geq 0, (D.1) shows that the restriction ψ⁡(t)=f⁡(t​𝐞3)+(ϱ/2)​t2\psi(t)=f(t\mathbf{e}_{3})+(\varrho/2)t^{2} satisfies

ψ−′​(0)=2LF>−2LF=ψ+′​(0),\psi^{\prime}_{-}(0)=\frac{2}{L_{F}}>-\frac{2}{L_{F}}=\psi^{\prime}_{+}(0),

contrary to the ordering of one-sided derivatives of a convex function. Thus no finite weak-convexity parameter is possible. ∎

This example concerns the interpolation family, not a separate low-dimensional query lower bound. It uses the directional assumptions of Lemma 3.2 directly, without invoking the cardinality condition of Lemma 3.1.
